newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: HOWARD SAYS HE'S COMMITTED TO SURCHARGE
The Prime Minister, John Howard, says he remains committed to the charge Government's proposed 15 per cent superannuation surcharge on high income earners.
His comments follow claims the surcharge is unconstitutional, and just another tax.

Former Attorney-General's Department Chief General, Counsel Dennis Rose QC, says the 15 per cent surcharge is plainly a tax. The Government will seek further legal advice on whether the surcharge is constitutional.
CONSUMER SENTIMENT RISES
The latest measure of consumer sentiment shows Australian consumers are still relatively pessimistic about economic prospects over the short and long terms.
The Westpac-Melbourne Institute Index of consumer sentiment rose by nearly five-per cent this month, reversing an eight-per cent drop in February.
However, Westpac's General Manager of Economics, Bill Evans, says in trend terms, consumer confidence remains steady.
And he says, more people seem to feel that now is a good time to buy major household items.
WOOLDRIDGE SAYS YOUNG DOCTORS WON'T WIN
Federal Health Minister, Michael Wooldridge, says the legislation over pathways to general practice is no longer open for debate, because it was passed last year.
Doctor Wooldridge says he has 22 vacancies for junior doctors, paying between 60 and 80-thousand dollars a year, which he can't fill.
He says if they have to move to finish their training, they'll still have the freedom to practice wherever they like at the end of it.
Doctor Wooldridge says the changes will improve the quality of general practice and get more GP's into rural areas.
SPECIAL BRANCH DISBANDED
The New South Wales Police Commissioner, Peter Ryan, today disbanded the state police services's Special Branch.
The move follows evidence given to the New South Wales Police Royal Commission involving the activities of the special branch.

This morning, just before the announcement, evidence was given at the Royal Commission that Special Branch had been keeping secret files on lawyers and civil libertarians, and had been investigating Sydney's Aboriginal community.

Commissioner Ryan says a review of the roles and responsibilities of the Police Special Branch has already begun, and some operational roles such as protection of VIPs and security assessments will continue to be carried out by other police.
Mr Ryan says the disbanding of the Police Special Branch will have no impact on security for the Sydney Olympics.
ALSTON SAYS MEDIA LAWS BEING REVIEWED
Communications Minister Richard Alston says the recent increase in foreign ownership of the Australian media, especially in print, is something the Government is looking at.
He's confirmed foreign ownership rules are being reviewed as part of the Government's review of Australia's media laws.
Senator Alston is finalising his proposed changes to existing cross media rules, that prevent media proprietors owning a newspaper and a television station in the one city.
The Minister says the review is also taking into account existing regulations that limit the stake in Australian media outlets available to foreigners.
ALSTON SAYS NOTHING EVIL IN OWNING OTHER MEDIA INTERESTS
The Communications Minister, Richard Alston, says he sees nothing inherently evil in media proprietors owning other non-media commercial interests, such as casinos.
Concern's been expressed about Nine Network owner, Kerry Packer, recently taking a controlling interest in the Sydney casino.
However Senator Alston has told the National Press Club in Canberra he could see nothing wrong with the move, as arrangements were in place to prevent any abuse of the situation.
WOMAN ATTEMPTS TO SUE NEW SOUTH WALES GOVT
An Aboriginal woman from the south coast of New South Wales has returned to the Supreme Court in Sydney in an attempt to sue the Government over her care more than fifty years ago.
54-year-old Joy Williams plans to sue the state of New South Wales after she was removed from her Aboriginal mother as a baby and placed in two different institutions in the 1940's.
She's alleging physical and mental abuse in one children's home and claims she was brought up to believe she was a white, orphan until aged in her early teens.
Her lawyer is today asking the Supreme Court for an expeditious hearing of the case.
UNI MARKETING STRATEGY SLAMMED BY UNION
The National Tertiary Education Union says a marketing program by the Central Queensland University to attract more high-fee paying foreign students is tacky and bizarre.
Union president, Dr Carolyn Allport, says the University is offering incentives such as free holidays and computers to overseas students, if they entice their friends to enrol.
Dr Allport says the program undermines the educational exchange that goes on between international students and Australian universities.
STEVEDORING INDUSTRY COMPETITION
Federal Transport minister John Sharp says new competition in stevedoring will make all waterfront operators more efficient.
At a Sydney waterfront industry conference Mr Sharp said new competitors won't have the stigma of high labour costs, bad work practices and bad culture associated with the industry.
He says new entrants to the market will strive to take business away from the two dominant existing stevedoring companies.
The Minister says that will force those companies to make full use of the new industrial laws.
Outside the conference, members of the Maritime Union passed out leaflets warning of the safety and environmental dangers of allowing foreign ships to ply domestic coastal routes.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
